description: Revived Bulgarian state (1185–1396) established by the Asen brothers' revolt against Byzantine overreach; at its Tarnovo-centred peak under Kaloyan and Ivan Asen II it controlled most of the Balkan peninsula and positioned itself as the successor empire to Byzantium, before internal dynastic conflict and Ottoman military pressure fractured its coherence and Tarnovo fell in 1393.

temporal.notes: Founded by Asen brothers' revolt; conquered by Ottomans

lifecycle_phases.description: Brothers Asen I and Peter lead a Bulgarian uprising against Byzantine tax increases; the Second Bulgarian Empire emerges from the Vlach-Bulgarian rebellion. Tsar Kaloyan (1197–1207) defeats and captures the Latin Emperor Baldwin I after the Fourth Crusade fragments Byzantine power.

Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) expands Bulgaria to its greatest medieval extent, controlling Albania, Macedonia, and Thrace. Battle of Klokotnitsa (1230) defeats the Epirote despot. Bulgaria becomes the dominant Balkan power until Mongol invasions destabilize the region.

Mongol tributaries, Byzantine resurgence, and then Ottoman expansion progressively reduce Bulgaria. The empire fragments into three rival states. Ottoman Sultan Murad I conquers Bulgaria systematically; the last Bulgarian tsar Ivan Shishman is captured and killed (1395).

rise_factors.description: Byzantine weakness after the Fourth Crusade (1204) created a power vacuum in the Balkans that the Asen brothers exploited; Latin Constantinople lacked the resources to reconquer the Balkans

Vlach-Bulgarian combined arms (cavalry + infantry) proved effective against Byzantine and later Latin forces; Ivan Asen II's campaigns showed sophisticated strategic planning across multiple Balkan theaters simultaneously

The Asen-Peter Uprising (1185) exploited Byzantine overextension. Brothers Peter and Asen mobilized Bulgarian peasants and Cuman allies, defeating Byzantine armies repeatedly and establishing Bulgarian independence within five years.

Bulgarian tsars systematically allied with Cuman steppe cavalry, providing a mobile strike force that neutralized Byzantine cavalry advantage. Cuman auxiliaries gave Bulgarian armies an offensive capability previously absent.

The Tarnovo Literary School, under Patriarch Euthymius (14th c.), produced major works of Slavic religious literature and developed the Church Slavonic orthographic reform that influenced Serbian and Russian literary traditions.

Ivan Asen II (r.1218–41) defeated the Despotate of Epirus at Klokotnitsa (1230), making Bulgaria the dominant Balkan power. His reign saw Bulgarian territorial expansion to three seas and a flowering of arts and commerce.

decline_factors.description: After Ivan Asen II's death, Bulgaria had 10 rulers in 30 years; boyar power and Mongol overlordship combined to prevent any strong central authority
Ottoman military expansion in the 14th century systematically conquered Bulgaria's Thracian territories; the empire fragmented into three rival states that Ottoman pressure eliminated one by one

Mongol raids (1240–42) devastated northern Bulgaria, killing population and disrupting agricultural production. Bulgaria became a Mongol tributary, with the Asen dynasty forced to send princes as hostages to the Khan's court.

After the Mongol weakening, Bulgarian boyars (noble landowners) progressively usurped central authority. By 1300, Bulgaria had effectively fragmented into semi-independent noble domains, making unified defense impossible.

Ottoman systematic conquest eliminated Bulgaria in stages: Tarnovo fell (1393), the last Bulgarian tsar was captured at Nicopolis (1396), and Vidin (1396) ended Bulgarian statehood. The country became an Ottoman province for nearly 500 years.

sources.author: Fine, John V.A., Jr.
sources.title: The Late Medieval Balkans: A Critical Survey from the Late Twelfth Century to the Ottoman Conquest
